new_statements.quote: § 29. Der Accent ruht auf einer der drei letzten Silben, in der Regel auf der vorletzten Silbe. Nach Castrén fällt der Ton auf die letzte Silbe des Wortes. a) Auf der vorletzten Silbe ruht der Accent in der Mehrzahl aller ostjakischen Grundformen ausser wenn die letzte Silbe lang und die vorletzte kurz ist, oder wenn die letzten zwei Silben eines mehrsilbigen Wortes kurz sind. [...] § 30. b) In der Regel ruht der Accent auf der letzten Silbe in zweisilbigen Wörtern, deren letzte Silbe lang und erste Silbe kurz ist [...] § 31. c) Auf der Antepenultima ruht der Accent selten und nur in mehrsilbigen Wörtern, deren zwei letzten Silben kurz sind
new_statements.translation: § 29. The accent rests on one of the last three syllables, as a rule on the penultimate syllable. According to Castrén the stress falls on the last syllable of the word. a) The accent rests on the penultimate syllable in the majority of all Ostyak base forms, except when the last syllable is long and the penult short, or when the last two syllables of a polysyllabic word are short. [...] § 30. b) As a rule the accent rests on the last syllable in disyllabic words whose last syllable is long and first syllable short [...] § 31. c) The accent rests on the antepenult rarely and only in polysyllabic words whose last two syllables are short

Nach Castrén fällt der Ton auf die letzte Silbe des Wortes. a) Auf der vorletzten Silbe ruht der Accent in der Mehrzahl aller ostjakischen Grundformen ausser wenn die letzte Silbe lang und die vorletzte kurz ist, oder wenn die letzten zwei Silben eines mehrsilbigen Wortes kurz sind'), §30 b) and §31 c) are on the page images word for word; the only deviations are scanned artefa…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls within a three-syllable window at the right edge of the word and is governed by vowel length: default penultimate; final when the final syllable is long and the penult short (also in some consonant-final nouns, loanwords and adverbs); antepenultimate when the last two syllables are both short (e.g. verbs with short suffixes -es, -eyed, -ed, -em). In polysyllables the penult is stressed only if long (long verbal suffixes such as -yamd, -as, -id count as long). Under inflection the accent tends to remain on the base-form syllable but moves to satisfy the rules (ablative -ivet, passive -aj-, 3Sg.Pret. -ot attract it).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described. Phrase level: a word used as a postposition carries only a weak accent (e.g. sarat' vatta 'over the sea': main stress on the first syllable of sarat', weak on vatta), enclitic particles have no accent of their own (§32 III-IV, p. 47).
new_statements.exceptions: Consonant-final nouns, adverbs and loanwords may take final stress even with a short final syllable (inar 'saddle', tabas, karap 'ship', taras 'merchant'), but 'almost as many' such words keep penultimate stress, so 'no general rule can be set up' and final-stressed words are marked in the dictionary (§30, p. 45); vowel-initial words follow the main rule except a few loans (yamd'e 'whip') and postposed adjectives (-kurpe, -surpe). Stress on syllables with only short vowels is weak and sometimes not clearly perceptible (§28, §32 II.1). Author explicitly contradicts Castrén 1858 (§51: stress 'in der Regel auf die letzte Silbe').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; stated for 'Grundformen' (citation/base forms) with a separate rule set for inflected forms (§32, pp. 45-47); covers the Irtysh, Demjanka and Konda dialects from Patkanov's 1880s-90s fieldwork; stress is not called distinctive. Later readings disagree: Castrén 1858 (Irtysh) gives final stress as the rule; Karjalainen 1905 treats initial stress as the unmarked default for all dialects; Normanskaja 2014 finds 1st/2nd-syllable, lexically assigned (paradigmatic) stress in Castrén's Irtysh manuscripts; Honti 1984 (general Khanty, second-hand) gives usually-initial stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Patkanov & Fuchs 1906 describe the 'süd-ostjakischen Dialekte' = Irtysh, Demjanka and upper/lower Konda Ostyak, i.e. exactly the extinct Southern Khanty group sout3226 (Glottolog lists no sub-dialect codes). Castrén 1858 is likewise Irtysh-based (with Surgut notes). Paasonen 1926 covers Konda (Southern) plus Jugan (Eastern, not sout3226). Normanskaja 2014 analyses Castrén's Irtysh manuscripts. None of the sources is a modern speaker-based description; the language died out in the 20th century.

sources.note: 'Accent und Quantität' §§28-33, pp. 43-47: accent lies on one of the last three syllables, as a rule the penult; final in disyllables with short first + long last syllable (and in some consonant-final nouns/loans/adverbs); antepenult only when the last two syllables are short; under inflection the accent tends to stay on the base-form syllable but shifts to obey these rules (ablative -ivet, passive -aj-, 3Sg.Pret -ot etc.); postpositions weakly stressed, enclitics unstressed.

sources.note: P. 284: in Castrén's Helsinki archive (~200 Irtysh Southern Khanty words) stress is marked on the 1st or 2nd syllable; infinitives always initial, oblique cases and 1Sg verb forms either; no dependence on vowel quality found, so a paradigmatic (lexically assigned) phonological stress is presumed for non-derived words. P. 301: place of stress in non-derived words identical in Irtysh (Castrén) and modern Nizyam. P. 283 quotes Honti 1984 (general Khanty): dynamic stress, usually initial, second syllable when the 1st vowel is reduced and the 2nd full, or when the 2nd is lower; not distinctive.

sources.citation: Castrén, M. Alexander. 1858. Versuch einer ostjakischen Sprachlehre nebst kurzem Wörterverzeichniss. 2nd ed., ed. Anton Schiefner (Nordische Reisen und Forschungen VI). St. Petersburg: Kaiserl. Akademie der Wissenschaften. (Grammar based on the Irtysh dialect, Vorwort p. VIII.)

sources.note: §51 p. 21: 'Was erstens den Ton betrifft, so hat er im Ostjakischen nicht immer dieselbe Stärke wie in den tatarischen Sprachen, fällt aber auch hier in der Regel auf die letzte Silbe des Worts.' Final stress strongest when the final vowel is long and the others short; weak when all syllables short and word vowel-final; a preceding long syllable weakens or removes the final-syllable stress (jógot, sódop).

sources.note: No descriptive references at all (only Schön 2014 subclassification comment, Campbell et al. 2022, Salminen 2000); status dormant/extinct.
Phonology section covers historical sound changes only; nothing on stress. Cites Csepregi 2023, Abondolo 1998, Honti 1998, Bakró-Nagy et al. 2022, Salminen 2023.

XVIII: 'Die quantität, wie übrigens auch der akzent, ist in den handschriften im allgemeinen sehr genau angegeben'; Paasonen's 1901 report (p.
